target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce scheduling barriers and help many people vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and retail/service work may continue as usual, so the holiday would not automatically reduce work or scheduling constraints for many voters.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would help low-income voters in particular.
objection: Because low-income workers are more likely to work retail and service jobs and may have to take unpaid time off or keep working, a federal Election Day holiday could disadvantage them rather than reliably improving their ability to vote.

target: AG1’s turnout argument for the holiday.
objection: Research shows that an election-day holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s suggestion that state-level reforms are not enough to replace a national holiday.
objection: State-level rules requiring employer time off to vote, along with automatic voter registration, directly address key barriers more reliably than a symbolic holiday.

target: AG1’s later claim that employers have no evidence of uniformly refusing scheduling accommodations on holidays.
objection: There is evidence that many private-sector employers, especially in retail and service, keep people scheduled on federal holidays and do not automatically provide the accommodations needed to vote, so the claim that there is no such evidence is unwarranted.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would help by reducing travel or commuting burden.
objection: Because private employers are not generally required to close on a federal holiday, most people would still commute normally, so traffic and travel around polling places would not meaningfully decrease for most voters.

target: AG1’s claim that weekend or holiday election days are a workable model for the U.S. and would not hurt low-income voters.
objection: Weekend or holiday election days can systematically leave low-income voters with work-based barriers, including wage loss and limited paid time, so they may actually worsen access for that group rather than help it.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would give low-income workers paid time to vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off, and low-income workers often work in jobs with limited paid leave, so they would not reliably get paid time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that many employers would likely provide paid holiday time or holiday pay that would let low-income workers vote.
objection: Retail and service work often continues on holidays, holiday pay can coexist with continued scheduling, and many low-income workers remain on shift during voting hours, so the holiday would not reliably translate into paid time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would reliably give many low-income workers paid voting time through holiday pay or closure.
objection: Many low-income workers are in part-time, temporary, or variable-hour roles that often do not qualify for paid holiday benefits, so a federal holiday would not reliably provide them paid time off to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that there is no evidence holiday designation is systematically ignored for low-income workers.
objection: There is evidence that federal holiday designation is often not translated into paid holiday time or holiday pay for low-income hourly workers, because many are still scheduled to work and do not receive those benefits automatically.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status would often translate into paid time or holiday pay allowing low-income workers to vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not legally require private employers to give time off to vote, and many low-income retail/service workers would still not be off during polling hours, so the core work barrier would often remain.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would reliably reduce work-based barriers and help many low-income hourly workers vote.
objection: Because a federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off during polling hours, it would not reliably remove the work-based voting barrier for low-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would also solve non-work barriers like childcare and transportation.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday mainly changes work and school schedules; it does not automatically solve childcare or transportation problems, which low-income families often face more acutely.

target: AG2’s claim that federal holiday status does not materially reduce scheduling barriers because private employers need not close or provide paid leave.
objection: Many private employers do treat federal holidays as days off or provide paid leave/holiday pay, so a federal Election Day holiday would reduce scheduling and wage-loss barriers for many workers even if it is not legally required everywhere.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would be disadvantaged by the holiday.
objection: A federal holiday can reduce the need for low-income workers to take unpaid time off or use scarce paid leave, so it is not inherently harmful to them and may actually ease their voting burden.

target: AG2’s claim that better alternatives like state time-off rules or automatic registration make a holiday unnecessary.
objection: Even if other reforms are also valuable, that does not mean a national holiday should be rejected; removing a major scheduling barrier is still a worthwhile policy reason to adopt it.

target: AG2’s assumption that employers uniformly refuse voting-related scheduling accommodations on national holidays.
objection: There is no evidence that employers uniformly refuse all scheduling accommodations for voting on national holidays, and a holiday can create expectations that make shift swaps or time-off requests easier.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not help low-income workers because childcare burdens remain.
objection: Many parents depend on school schedules for childcare, and a holiday would reduce those childcare and logistics barriers, which are especially burdensome for low-income working families.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not matter because it is only symbolic.
objection: Making voting feel like a civic celebration rather than a chore can elevate civic participation and increase people’s sense that voting matters, which supports turnout and democracy.

target: AG2’s argument that state-level reforms are better because they are more targeted.
objection: State laws vary across states and cannot uniformly fix scheduling barriers nationwide, while a federal holiday would apply across all states on the same day and more consistently reduce barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that commuting and traffic would not improve on Election Day.
objection: National holidays usually reduce weekday commuting and traffic, so a federal Election Day holiday could reduce travel-time burdens for voters heading to polling places.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday election days systematically worsen access for low-income voters.
objection: Peer democracies commonly hold elections on weekends or holidays, which suggests that holiday elections are workable and do not inherently disadvantage low-income voters.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not reliably provide paid voting time to low-income workers.
objection: Many private employers do treat federal holidays as days off or provide holiday pay, so a holiday would often give low-income workers paid time or paid leave during voting hours.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday pay does not equal time off and therefore does not help voting.
objection: If workers receive paid holiday time, holiday pay, or are scheduled off during the polling window, they can vote without wage loss, so the holiday can still provide meaningful paid voting time.

target: AG2’s claim that many low-income workers would not qualify for paid holiday benefits.
objection: Even if not every worker qualifies, many private workplaces still observe federal holidays with paid leave or holiday pay, so the holiday would often create paid voting time for many low-income hourly workers.

target: AG2’s claim that many workplaces ignore federal holidays for low-income workers.
objection: Many private workplaces do observe federal holidays through closure, paid leave, or holiday pay, so the claim that holiday designation is generally ignored for these workers overstates the case.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday would not reliably remove work-based barriers.
objection: Because many employers would provide closure, paid leave, or holiday compensation, a federal Election Day holiday would often reduce work-based barriers and make voting easier for many low-income workers.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not justified because it would not increase turnout enough and better reforms exist.
objection: A policy can be justified even if it is not the single most effective reform, and removing a major barrier still helps participation; therefore the holiday can still be a worthwhile national policy.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not reliably remove key barriers for low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday would often create paid time off or holiday pay and reduce scheduling barriers for many low-income workers, so it does meaningfully improve access rather than leaving the barrier intact in all cases.
